Confidence-Based Decoding is Provably Efficient
for Diffusion Language Models00footnotetext: Corresponding author: Gen Li.

Changxiao Cai ††thanks: Department of Industrial and Operations Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, USA; Email: cxcai@umich.edu.    Gen Li ††thanks: Department of Statistics and Data Science, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Email: genli@cuhk.edu.hk.
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Diffusion language models (DLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive (AR) models for language modeling, allowing flexible generation order and parallel generation of multiple tokens. However, this flexibility introduces a challenge absent in AR models: the decoding strategy—which determines the order and number of tokens generated at each iteration—critically affects sampling efficiency. Among decoding strategies explored in practice, confidence-based methods, which adaptively select which and how many tokens to unmask based on prediction confidence, have shown strong empirical performance. Despite this success, our theoretical understanding of confidence-based decoding remains limited.

In this work, we develop the first theoretical analysis framework for confidence-based decoding in DLMs. We focus on an entropy sum-based strategy that continues unmasking tokens within each iteration until the cumulative entropy exceeds a threshold, and show that it achieves ε\varepsilon-accurate sampling in KL divergence with an expected number of iterations O~​(H​(X0)/ε)\widetilde{O}(H(X_{0})/\varepsilon), where H⁡(X0)H(X_{0}) denotes the entropy of the target data distribution. Notably, this strategy yields substantial sampling acceleration when the data distribution has low entropy relative to the sequence length, while automatically adapting to the intrinsic complexity of data without requiring prior knowledge or hyperparameter tuning. Overall, our results provide a theoretical foundation for confidence-based decoding and may inform the design of more efficient decoding strategies for DLMs.

Keywords: diffusion language model, confidence-based decoding, iteration complexity, information theory

1 Introduction

Diffusion language models (DLMs) (Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024) have recently emerged as a compelling alternative to the autoregressive (AR) paradigm for language modeling. Unlike AR models, DLMs use a non-causal generation mechanism that can produce multiple tokens in parallel at each iteration and relax the rigid left-to-right constraint. The parallel generation capability offers strong potential for sampling acceleration, while the non-causal structure also makes DLMs well suited to tasks that benefit from bidirectional reasoning or the enforcement of global constraints (Nie et al., 2025; Prabhudesai et al., 2025). At scale, DLMs have been shown to achieve performance competitive with AR models (Ye et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025; You et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Bie et al., 2025; Labs et al., 2025).

State-of-the-art DLMs are built upon masked diffusion models (MDMs) (Austin et al., 2021; Campbell et al., 2022; Lou et al., 2023), a class of discrete diffusion models that augment the vocabulary with an additional absorbing state, referred to as mask. An MDM is defined through two complementary processes. In the forward (masking) process, tokens in a sequence drawn from the target data distribution are progressively replaced by the mask until the sequence becomes fully masked. The reverse (unmasking) process then seeks to invert this corruption by iteratively recovering masked tokens, thereby transforming a fully masked sequence into a fresh sample from the data distribution.

Central to the reverse process is a mask predictor, which learns the conditional distributions of masked tokens given the currently unmasked context at various masking levels (Lou et al., 2023; Ou et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024). The reverse dynamics are implemented by repeatedly sampling token values from these conditionals to impute masked positions, thereby moving from a fully masked sequence toward a data-like sample. In this sense, the mask predictor in MDMs serves as a discrete analog of the score estimator in continuous diffusion models (Song et al., 2020). As the joint distribution of multiple masked tokens is generally intractable in high-dimensional settings, practical mask predictors are typically trained to learn the conditional marginals of each masked token, and use the product of per-token conditional marginals as an approximation (Nie et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). In particular, a neural network-based mask predictor can output, in one forward pass, conditional marginal distributions for all currently masked positions.

While this factorized approximation enables parallel generation of DLMs, it also introduces an inevitable bias in the sampling stage—simultaneously unmasking multiple tokens in one iteration ignores their statistical dependence conditioned on the currently revealed context. At one extreme, unmasking all tokens in a single iteration incurs an error comparable to the discrepancy between the target distribution and the product of its marginals. At the other extreme, generating tokens one-by-one recovers the standard AR approach, which removes the factorization bias but sacrifices the parallel generation advantage of DLMs.

Therefore, the sampling speed and generation quality of DLMs depend critically on the decoding (or unmasking) strategy used at the inference stage, which determines both which positions to unmask and how many tokens to reveal at each iteration.

Parallel decoding strategies.

Decoding strategies used in practice can be broadly categorized into two families.

  • •

    Uniform decoding strategies. This class of decoding strategies prescribes a fixed total iteration count TT and a step-size schedule s1,s2​…,sTs_{1},s_{2}\dots,s_{T} with st≥1s_{t}\geq 1 and ∑t=1Tst=L\sum_{t=1}^{T}s_{t}=L (e.g., cosine schedules (Shi et al., 2024) or log-linear schedules (Sahoo et al., 2024; Lou et al., 2023)). At each iteration tt, one samples a subset of size sts_{t} uniformly at random from the remaining masked positions and then unmasks the tokens in the sampled subset. Note that this family of schemes treats all masked positions uniformly and thus belongs to the broader class of non-adaptive decoding strategies.

  • •

    Confidence-based decoding strategies. This collection of decoding strategies leverages the fact that a mask predictor provides not only a distribution but also a natural confidence signal for each token prediction. It is thus natural to unmask the “easiest” tokens first—those predicted with high confidence—so that newly revealed tokens can serve as additional context for the harder ones in later iterations (Chang et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2023; Gong et al., 2024). In practice, confidence is often quantified by the entropy of the predicted distribution (Ben-Hamu et al., 2025), the mass of the most likely token (Nie et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025), or the likelihood gap between the two most likely tokens (Kim et al., 2025), leading to a range of effective heuristics. Compared to uniform decoding strategies, these schemes determine the decoding order and batch size in an adaptive manner.

In contrast to the rapid development of empirical decoding strategies, our theoretical understanding of their sampling efficiency remains limited. For uniform random schedules, substantial recent progress has been made in establishing theoretical guarantees for sampling performance (Li and Cai, 2025; Chen et al., 2025b; Lavenant and Zanella, 2025; Dmitriev et al., 2026; Zhao and Cai, 2026). We defer a detailed discussion to Section 1.2. By comparison, despite their strong empirical performance, confidence-based decoding remains far less understood theoretically. The fundamental difficulty lies in their inherently adaptive decoding dynamics: the set of tokens unmasked at each iteration depends on the realization of the tokens generated so far, through the corresponding confidence levels produced by the mask predictor. This adaptivity raises several fundamental but unanswered questions. For instance, if the total number of iterations is not predetermined, how many iterations are needed to unmask all tokens? What is the resulting sampling error? Can these schemes provably adapt to the (unknown) intrinsic complexity or dependence structure of the data distribution?

Such a theory-practice gap motivates the central question of our study:

Are confidence-based decoding strategies in DLMs provably efficient?

1.1 Our contributions

In this work, we take an initial step toward answering this question by developing sampling convergence guarantees for confidence-based decoding in DLMs, with the goal of demystifying their practical effectiveness.

We focus on a canonical confidence measure—entropy—and investigate entropy-based decoding that selects unmasking positions and batch sizes based on the entropy of the predicted distribution at each masked position. Concretely, we study a representative entropy sum-based strategy that, at each iteration, greedily unmasks tokens from the remaining masked positions until the running entropy sum of the newly unmasked tokens exceeds a prescribed threshold, thereby revealing as many tokens as possible per iteration while keeping the cumulative prediction uncertainty controlled.

We demonstrate that ε\varepsilon-accuracy in Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence can be attained with an expected number of iterations that scales as

O~​(H⁡(X0)ε).\displaystyle\widetilde{O}\bigg(\frac{H(X_{0})}{\varepsilon}\bigg).

This result implies a sublinear iteration complexity in the sequence length LL when the data distribution has low entropy H⁡(X0)≪LH(X_{0})\ll L, thereby achieving provable sampling speedup compared to the Θ⁡(L)\Theta(L) iteration complexity of the AR decoding or naive uniform parallel decoding. Notably, this scheme does not require any prior knowledge of the data distribution such as its entropy, and thus automatically adapts to the intrinsic low-complexity data structure to achieve sampling acceleration.

To establish these results, we introduce a novel analysis framework for adaptive decoding dynamics in DLMs that may be of independent interest. Overall, our results provide the first theoretical justification for the effectiveness of confidence-based unmasking strategies, and offer a principled explanation of when and why entropy-based decoding can achieve accelerated sampling without sacrificing generation fidelity. Our theoretical insights may inform the design of more efficient inference schemes in practice.

1.2 Other related work

Convergence theory for uniform decoding strategies.

Existing sampling convergence analysis for DLMs largely focuses on uniform decoding strategies and two main viewpoints have been pursued. The first line of work directly studies the sampling error accumulated in the iterative unmasking procedure under the factorized approximation. For balanced step-size schedules (i.e., st≍L/Ts_{t}\asymp L/T for all tt), Li and Cai (2025) established an O⁡(1/T)O(1/T) convergence rate in KL divergence, with leading factor equal to the sum of mutual information ∑i=1TI⁡(Xi,X∖i)\sum_{i=1}^{T}I(X^{i};X^{\smallsetminus i}) between the ii-th token XiX^{i} and the remaining tokens X∖i≔(Xj)j≠iX^{\smallsetminus i}\coloneqq(X^{j})_{j\neq i} under the data distribution. They also proved matching lower bounds (up to constant factors), showing that the O⁡(1/T)O(1/T) decay is unimprovable for balanced step-size schedules in the worst case. Subsequently, Chen et al. (2025b) refined the convergence rate using the total correlation and dual total correlation of the data distribution, and developed optimal step-size schedules. These schedules can outperform balanced step-size schedules, albeit requiring either a priori estimates of these correlation measures or hyperparameter tuning. Recently, Zhao and Cai (2026) showed that randomized step-size schedules can automatically adapt to intrinsic dependence structure underlying data, leading to improved iteration complexity for structured data distributions. A parallel viewpoint analyzes discrete diffusion models from the perspective of CTMC discretization. However, most results in this direction yield iteration complexity that scales at least linearly in the sequence length (Chen and Ying, 2024; Liang et al., 2025b; Feng et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2026). Consequently, they fail to capture the parallel-generation regime in DLM decoding. A notable exception is Dmitriev et al. (2026), which developed sharp and adaptive guarantees for MDMs, with convergence rate governed by low-complexity measures of data.

Empirical confidence-based strategies.

Early confidence-based approaches typically use a fixed-size strategy, which prescribes an unmasking size KK and unmasks the top-KK most confident tokens at each iteration (Chang et al., 2022). This idea has been instantiated with several ranking criteria, including top-KK probability (Nie et al., 2025), top-KK margin (Kim et al., 2025), and top-KK entropy (Ben-Hamu et al., 2025). More recent work considers adaptive strategies, where the number of newly unmasked tokens is determined on the fly. Examples include threshold-based rules that reveal tokens whose confidence exceeds a prescribed level (Yu et al., 2025), and budget-based strategies that continue unmasking while the accumulated uncertainty remains within a budget (Ben-Hamu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). The methods analyzed in this paper fall into this category. Beyond those one-step confidence rules, several works combine confidence information with more structured decoding procedures. For instance, Wei et al. (2025) proposes a two-stage method that alternates between exploratory and accelerated decoding strategies depending on the confidence region. In addition, another line of work seeks to improve decoding by explicitly planning ahead for future iterations rather than making purely myopic decisions, including lookahead-based exploration methods (Fu et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2025) and trial-and-verification procedures (Wu and Zhang, 2025; Li et al., 2026). Finally, to mitigate the limitation of standard MDMs that fix tokens once they are unmasked, recent work has also studied confidence-based remasking mechanisms that allow low-confidence tokens to be revised in later iterations (Wang et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2024).

Theory for continuous diffusion models.

A rich body of work has developed sampling convergence guarantees for continuous diffusion models in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (Lee et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023a; Benton et al., 2023; Li and Yan, 2024b; Li et al., 2024b), with state-of-the-art iteration complexity of O~​(d/ε)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d/\varepsilon}) in KL divergence and O~​(d/ε)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d}/\varepsilon) in total variation distance (Jiao et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). A variety of provably accelerated samplers have been further developed (Li and Cai, 2024; Li and Jiao, 2024; Gatmiry et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2025b). A theme relevant to our work is the adaptivity to (unknown) low-complexity structure. Several recent works (Li and Yan, 2024a; Liang et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2024b; Potaptchik et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a) show that when the data distribution concentrates near a kk-dimensional structure with k≪dk\ll d, the dependence on the ambient dimension dd can be replaced by the intrinsic dimension kk, yielding substantial sampling acceleration. Beyond sampling convergence, end-to-end statistical guarantees have been developed to demonstrate the optimality of diffusion-based distribution learning and sample generation (Oko et al., 2023; Wibisono et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Cai and Li, 2025; Gatmiry et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024). Further results tailored to structured data have also been established, including distributions supported on low-dimensional linear subspaces or manifolds (Chen et al., 2023b; Tang and Yang, 2024; Azangulov et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Yakovlev and Puchkin, 2025), distributions with low-complexity dependence (Fan et al., 2025), and factor models (Chen et al., 2025a).

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we provide an overview of the fundamental concepts underlying DLMs.

Forward (masking) process.

Consider a token sequence X0=(X01,X02,…,X0L)∈𝕏LX_{0}=(X^{1}_{0},X^{2}_{0},\dots,X^{L}_{0})\in\mathbb{X}^{L} sampled from the data distribution p𝖽𝖺𝗍𝖺p_{\mathsf{data}}. The forward process progressively corrupts X0X_{0} by replacing its tokens with the mask symbol 𝖬\mathsf{M} until the entire sequence is masked. Formally, let XtX_{t} denote the partially masked sequence obtained after tt masking steps and let ℳt≔{i∈[L]:Xti=𝖬}\mathcal{M}_{t}\coloneqq\{i\in[L]\colon X_{t}^{i}=\mathsf{M}\} denote the index set of masked tokens. At each step t≥1t\geq 1, we select a masking set 𝒮t⊆[L]∖ℳt−1\mathcal{S}_{t}\subseteq[L]\setminus\mathcal{M}_{t-1} and update Xt−1X_{t-1} to XtX_{t} by replacing tokens at positions in the set 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} with 𝖬\mathsf{M}:

Xti={𝖬,if ​i∈𝒮t,Xt−1i,if ​i∉𝒮t.\displaystyle X_{t}^{i}=\begin{cases}\mathsf{M},&\text{if }i\in\mathcal{S}_{t},\\ X_{t-1}^{i},&\text{if }i\notin\mathcal{S}_{t}.\end{cases}

The masking process continues until all tokens have been masked.

Mask predictor training.

DLMs are trained to reverse the above forward masking process by learning the conditional distribution of masked tokens given the unmasked ones. A notable feature of mask predictor training is that this posterior distribution is time-independent—it depends only on the unmasked context and not on the masking step tt (Ou et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024). More precisely, for each token index i∈[L]i\in[L] and any set of unmasked positions 𝒮⊆[L]∖{i}\mathcal{S}\subseteq[L]\setminus\{i\}, we define the true conditional marginal distribution of X0iX^{i}_{0} given X0𝒮X_{0}^{\mathcal{S}} under the data distribution p𝖽𝖺𝗍𝖺p_{\mathsf{data}} as

pi​(x∣z𝒮)≔ℙ⁡{X0i=x∣X0𝒮=z𝒮}∀x∈𝕏,z𝒮∈𝕏|𝒮|.\displaystyle p^{i}(x\mid z^{\mathcal{S}})\coloneqq\mathbb{P}\big\{X_{0}^{i}=x\mid X_{0}^{\mathcal{S}}=z^{\mathcal{S}}\big\}\qquad\forall\,x\in\mathbb{X},\,z^{\mathcal{S}}\in\mathbb{X}^{|\mathcal{S}|}. (4)

The objective is to learn estimators pθi(⋅∣⋅)p^{i}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\cdot) for each conditional marginal pi(⋅∣⋅)p^{i}(\cdot\mid\cdot), thereby forming a mask predictor pθ=∏i=1Lpθip_{\theta}=\prod_{i=1}^{L}p^{i}_{\theta}.

The mask predictor is trained by maximizing the log-likelihood of masked tokens conditioned on unmasked ones:

maxpθ=∏i=1Lpθi⁡𝔼X0,𝒮​[1|𝒮c|​∑i∈𝒮clog⁡pθi​(X0i∣X0𝒮)].\displaystyle\max_{p_{\theta}=\prod_{i=1}^{L}p_{\theta}^{i}}\mathbb{E}_{X_{0},\mathcal{S}}\Bigg[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{c}}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{c}}}\log p^{i}_{\theta}\big(X_{0}^{i}\mid X_{0}^{\mathcal{S}}\big)\Bigg]. (5)

This objective is equivalent to minimizing the KL divergence between the data distribution and the distribution induced by the product of learned conditional marginals over partially masked sequences. In practice, the expectation is approximated by averaging over a finite number of training samples and random masking patterns.

We remark that the product of the true conditional marginals ∏i=1Lpi\prod_{i=1}^{L}p^{i} defined in (4) is the maximizer of the training objective (5).

Reverse (unmasking) process.

Given a trained mask predictor pθp_{\theta}, DLMs produce a token sequence through an iterative unmasking procedure. Starting from a fully masked sequence Y0=(𝖬,𝖬,…,𝖬)∈𝕏¯LY_{0}=(\mathsf{M},\mathsf{M},\ldots,\mathsf{M})\in\overline{\mathbb{X}}^{L} with cumulative unmasking set 𝒲0=∅\mathcal{W}_{0}=\varnothing, we repeat the following two steps for iteration t=1,2,…t=1,2,\dots until all tokens have been unmasked.

  1. 1.

    Select unmasking set. Choose a subset 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} of the currently masked positions [L]∖𝒲t−1[L]\setminus\mathcal{W}_{t-1} according to a decoding strategy, and update the cumulative unmasking set 𝒲t=𝒲t−1∪𝒟t\mathcal{W}_{t}=\mathcal{W}_{t-1}\cup\mathcal{D}_{t}.

  2. 2.

    Sample tokens. Draw the tokens for all positions in 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} independently and simultaneously from the learned mask predictor pθ=∏i=1Lpθip_{\theta}=\prod_{i=1}^{L}p_{\theta}^{i}, namely,

    Y^i∼pθi(⋅∣Yt−1),∀i∈𝒟t.\displaystyle\widehat{Y}^{i}\sim p_{\theta}^{i}\big(\cdot\mid Y_{t-1}\big),\quad\forall\,i\in\mathcal{D}_{t}. (6)

    The sequence is then updated by inserting the newly sampled tokens:

    Yti={Y^i,if ​i∈𝒟t,Yt−1i,if ​i∉𝒟t.\displaystyle Y_{t}^{i}=\begin{cases}\widehat{Y}^{i},&\text{if }i\in\mathcal{D}_{t},\\ Y_{t-1}^{i},&\text{if }i\notin\mathcal{D}_{t}.\end{cases} (7)

The final output is the fully unmasked sequence YT∈𝕏LY_{T}\in\mathbb{X}^{L}, where TT is the (potentially random) number of iterations.

It is worth noting that given a fixed mask predictor pθp_{\theta}, the sampling process of DLMs and the sampled distribution pYTp_{Y_{T}} are completely determined by the choice of decoding strategy, which specifies the unmasking set 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} at each iteration tt.

3 Main results

In this section, we present two entropy-based decoding strategies for DLMs and establish their theoretical guarantees. We begin with the entropy sum-based strategy, which is the main algorithmic result of the paper, and then study a maximum entropy-based variant to illustrate how the choice of entropy criterion affects sampling efficiency.

3.1 Entropy sum-based decoding strategy

We first introduce the entropy sum-based decoding strategy. Its key feature is that each decoding iteration is determined by the total uncertainty, measured by entropy, accumulated over the current batch of unmasked tokens. This leads to an adaptive rule that enlarges the unmasking set automatically in low-uncertainty regions and shrinks it when the mask predictor is uncertain.

Decoding procedure.

At a high level, the entropy sum-based strategy scans the remaining masked positions in a random order and continues unmasking tokens until the cumulative entropy of the current batch exceeds a threshold.

Concretely, we first draw a permutation Π\Pi of [L][L] uniformly at random, where Πk\Pi_{k} represents the index of the kk-th token to be unmasked. We then repeat the following decoding procedure until all tokens have been generated. At each iteration t≥1t\geq 1, we initialize the current unmasking set 𝒟t=∅\mathcal{D}_{t}=\varnothing and the running entropy sum S=0S=0. Recall that for any set 𝒲\mathcal{W}, we use the upper-case letter W=|𝒲|W=|\mathcal{W}| to denote its size. Given the partially unmasked sequence Yt−1Y_{t-1} from the previous iteration, in which the tokens indexed by the cumulative unmasking set

𝒲t−1=⋃i=1t−1𝒟i={Π1,…,ΠWt−1}\mathcal{W}_{t-1}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{t-1}\mathcal{D}_{i}=\big\{\Pi_{1},\ldots,\Pi_{W_{t-1}}\big\}

have been generated, we continue along the permutation and examine the positions Πk\Pi_{k} for

k=Wt−1+1,Wt−1+2,…\displaystyle k=W_{t-1}+1,W_{t-1}+2,\dots

For each such position Πk\Pi_{k}, we compute the entropy of the corresponding conditional marginal pθΠk(⋅∣Yt−1)p^{\Pi_{k}}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid Y_{t-1}), generate the token YtΠkY_{t}^{\Pi_{k}} from this marginal, add the index Πk\Pi_{k} to the current unmasking set 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}, and update the running entropy sum SS by 𝙷(pθΠk(⋅∣Yt−1))\mathtt{H}\big(p^{\Pi_{k}}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid Y_{t-1})\big)11 1 Here, we use the notation 𝙷\mathtt{H} defined in (2) to denote the pointwise conditional entropy. It is a random variable depending on Yt−1Y_{t-1}, as opposed to the standard conditional entropy HH that averages over the randomness in Yt−1Y_{t-1}..

The iteration terminates once the running entropy sum SS exceeds a prescribed threshold η\eta or all LL tokens have been generated. Equivalently, the index set of newly unmasked tokens at iteration tt has the form

𝒟t={Πk:Wt−1<k≤kt},\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{t}=\big\{\Pi_{k}\colon W_{t-1}<k\leq k_{t}\big\},

where ktk_{t} is defined by

kt≔min{i>Wt−1:∑k=Wt−1+1i𝙷(pθΠk(⋅∣Yt−1))>η}∧L.\displaystyle k_{t}\coloneqq\min\biggl\{i>W_{t-1}:\sum_{k=W_{t-1}+1}^{i}\mathtt{H}\big(p^{\Pi_{k}}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid Y_{t-1})\big)>\eta\biggr\}\wedge L.

In other words, ktk_{t} is the first permutation index beyond Wt−1W_{t-1} such that the cumulative entropy over permutation indices k=Wt−1+1,…,ktk=W_{t-1}+1,\ldots,k_{t} exceeds η\eta, or LL if no such index appears before the sequence is fully unmasked.

The complete decoding procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1.

Remark 1.

The random permutation Π\Pi is introduced solely to simplify the presentation and analysis. Equivalently, the algorithm may be viewed as selecting the next token from the remaining masked positions uniformly at random.

An important observation is that, for each iteration tt, conditioned on the permutation Π\Pi, the cumulative unmasking set 𝒲t−1\mathcal{W}_{t-1}, and the partially unmasked sequence Yt−1Y_{t-1}, the unmasking set 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} (and thus the cumulative unmasking set 𝒲t=𝒲t−1∪𝒟t\mathcal{W}_{t}=\mathcal{W}_{t-1}\cup\mathcal{D}_{t}) is fully determined by the conditional entropies:

𝙷(pθΠk(⋅∣Yt−1)),k=Wt−1+1,Wt−1+2,…,L.\displaystyle\mathtt{H}\big(p^{\Pi_{k}}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid Y_{t-1})\big),\quad k=W_{t-1}+1,W_{t-1}+2,\dots,L.

Once 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} is determined, we obtain the iterate YtY_{t} by generating the tokens in 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} independently according to the corresponding conditional distributions

Yti∼pθi(⋅∣Yt−1),i∈𝒟t,Y_{t}^{i}\sim p^{i}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid Y_{t-1}),\quad i\in\mathcal{D}_{t},

or equivalently,

YtΠk∼pθΠk(⋅∣Yt−1),Wt−1+1≤k≤Wt.Y_{t}^{\Pi_{k}}\sim p^{\Pi_{k}}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid Y_{t-1}),\quad W_{t-1}+1\leq k\leq W_{t}.

Therefore, the overall sampling process can be summarized by the following Markov chain:

Π→{𝙷(pθΠk(⋅∣Y0))}k=1L→(𝒟1,𝒲1)→Y1→{𝙷(pθΠk(⋅∣Y1))}k=W1+1L→(𝒟2,𝒲2)→Y2\displaystyle\Pi\to\bigl\{\mathtt{H}\big(p^{\Pi_{k}}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid Y_{0})\big)\bigr\}_{k=1}^{L}\to(\mathcal{D}_{1},\mathcal{W}_{1})\to Y_{1}\to\bigl\{\mathtt{H}\big(p^{\Pi_{k}}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid Y_{1})\big)\bigr\}_{k=W_{1}+1}^{L}\to(\mathcal{D}_{2},\mathcal{W}_{2})\to Y_{2}
→…→{𝙷(pθΠk(⋅∣YT−1))}k=WT−1+1L→(𝒟T,𝒲T)→YT,\displaystyle\qquad\to\dots\to\bigl\{\mathtt{H}\big(p^{\Pi_{k}}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid Y_{T-1})\big)\bigr\}_{k=W_{T-1}+1}^{L}\to(\mathcal{D}_{T},\mathcal{W}_{T})\to Y_{T}, (8)

where TT denotes the (random) total number of iterations.

Connection to empirical entropy sum-based strategies.

Algorithm 1 is closely related to the entropy-based decoding strategy recently proposed in Ben-Hamu et al. (2025). Their method sorts the remaining tokens by conditional entropy and then selects the largest subset for which the gap between the entropy sum and the maximum entropy remains below a prescribed threshold. Numerical results in Ben-Hamu et al. (2025) demonstrate that such an entropy sum-based decoding strategy achieves considerable speedups in generation, with quality that matches or surpasses that of uniform unmasking schemes. The main difference is that Algorithm 1 scans token positions in a random order instead of a deterministic entropy-sorted order. We introduce this randomness primarily to facilitate the theoretical analysis, and it would be of interest to investigate whether similar theoretical guarantees can be established for the deterministic variants.

3.2 Theoretical guarantee

We now state the performance guarantee for the entropy sum-based decoding scheme (Algorithm 1) in Theorem 1. The proof sketch can be found in Section 4.2.

Theorem 1.

Assume that the mask predictor pθp_{\theta} is optimal, namely, pθ=∏i=1Lpip_{\theta}=\prod_{i=1}^{L}p^{i} is the product of true conditional marginals. For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, set the threshold to η=ε/(4​(log2⁡L+1))\eta=\varepsilon/\big(4(\log_{2}L+1)\big). Then the entropy sum-based strategy in Algorithm 1 achieves ε\varepsilon-accurate sampling in KL divergence, i.e., 𝔼Π[𝖪𝖫(pX0∥pYT|Π)]≤ε.\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}\big[\mathsf{KL}(p_{X_{0}}\parallel p_{Y_{T}\mid\Pi})\big]\leq\varepsilon. Moreover, the expected number of iterations satisfies

𝔼⁡[T]≤4​(H⁡(X0)ε+1)​(log2⁡L+1)+1,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[T]\leq 4\bigg(\frac{H(X_{0})}{\varepsilon}+1\bigg)(\log_{2}L+1)+1, (9)

where H⁡(X0)H(X_{0}) denotes the entropy of the target data distribution.

To the best of our knowledge, this result provides the first theoretical guarantee for confidence-based decoding strategies in DLMs. We discuss several important implications below.

  • •

    Iteration complexity. The expected number of iterations required to achieve ε\varepsilon-accuracy in KL divergence is at most

    O~​(H⁡(X0)ε).\displaystyle\widetilde{O}\bigg(\frac{H(X_{0})}{\varepsilon}\bigg). (10)

    Up to a logarithmic dependence on the sequence length LL, this iteration complexity depends only on the entropy of the target data distribution, which can be viewed as a measure of its intrinsic complexity. Consequently, when the target distribution has low entropy, namely H⁡(X0)≪LH(X_{0})\ll L, the entropy sum-based decoding scheme yields a substantial sampling speedup.

  • •

    Adaptivity to intrinsic structure. The above sampling acceleration is achieved without requiring any prior knowledge of the data distribution or hyperparameter tuning. This highlights the distribution-agnostic adaptivity of the entropy-based decoding—it automatically exploits low-complexity structure in the target distribution to accelerate generation.

3.3 Effect of entropy criterion

A natural question is how the choice of entropy criterion affects decoding efficiency. To investigate this, we present a second entropy-based decoding strategy—the maximum entropy-based strategy—which differs from the entropy sum-based strategy in a single design choice. Instead of controlling the cumulative entropy of the entire batch, it terminates an iteration as soon as any single token’s conditional entropy exceeds a prescribed threshold, subject to an explicit cap on the batch size.

As we will see shortly, this alternative strategy still achieves an iteration complexity sublinear in the sequence length. However, its sampling guarantee is weaker in two respects: the iteration complexity bound is looser, and the parameter choice requires knowledge of the entropy of the target distribution. This contrast highlights the importance of how entropy is incorporated into the design of decoding strategies.

Maximum entropy-based decoding strategy.

As before, we begin by drawing a random permutation Π\Pi of [L][L]. At iteration t≥1t\geq 1, given the previous iterate Yt−1Y_{t-1} with cumulative unmasking set 𝒲t−1\mathcal{W}_{t-1}, we scan the remaining positions in the permutation order and keep adding them to the current batch 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}. The iteration ends as soon as one of the following occurs:

  1. (i)

    the entropy of the most recently unmasked token exceeds the threshold η\eta (this token is included in the set 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t});

  2. (ii)

    the current batch reaches the cap size SmaxS_{\max};

  3. (iii)

    all LL tokens have been generated.

Formally, the index set 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} of newly unmasked tokens at iteration tt is given by

𝒟t={Πk:Wt−1<k≤kt},\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{t}=\big\{\Pi_{k}\colon W_{t-1}<k\leq k_{t}\big\},

where ktk_{t} is the first permutation index after Wt−1W_{t-1} for which the entropy exceeds η\eta, or Wt−1+SmaxW_{t-1}+S_{\max} if no such index appears within the next SmaxS_{\max} positions, or LL if no such index appears before all tokens are generated. In other words, ktk_{t} is defined by

kt≔min{i>Wt−1:𝙷(pθΠi(⋅∣Yt−1))>η}∧(Wt−1+Smax)∧L.\displaystyle k_{t}\coloneqq\min\bigl\{i>W_{t-1}:\mathtt{H}\big(p^{\Pi_{i}}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid Y_{t-1})\big)>\eta\bigr\}\wedge(W_{t-1}+S_{\max})\wedge L.

A complete description of the unmasking scheme is given in Algorithm 2.

Compared with the entropy sum-based decoding scheme, this strategy differs only in the stopping criterion:

  1. 1.

    it reacts to the entropy of a single token rather than the cumulative entropy of the whole batch;

  2. 2.

    it explicitly imposes a maximum unmasking size SmaxS_{\max}.

Despite this difference, these two entropy-based strategies share the same Markovian structure: the unmasking sets 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} and 𝒲t\mathcal{W}_{t} at iteration tt are fully determined by the previous iterate Yt−1Y_{t-1} together with its cumulative unmasking set 𝒲t−1\mathcal{W}_{t-1}. Accordingly, the sampling process under the maximum entropy-based decoding scheme also forms a Markov chain as follows:

Π→{𝙷(pθΠk(⋅∣Y0))}k=1L→(𝒟1,𝒲1)→Y1→{𝙷(pθΠk(⋅∣Y1))}k=W1+1L→(𝒟2,𝒲2)→Y2\displaystyle\Pi\to\bigl\{\mathtt{H}\big(p^{\Pi_{k}}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid Y_{0})\big)\bigr\}_{k=1}^{L}\to(\mathcal{D}_{1},\mathcal{W}_{1})\to Y_{1}\to\bigl\{\mathtt{H}\big(p^{\Pi_{k}}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid Y_{1})\big)\bigr\}_{k=W_{1}+1}^{L}\to(\mathcal{D}_{2},\mathcal{W}_{2})\to Y_{2}
→…→{𝙷(pθΠk(⋅∣YT−1))}k=WT−1+1L→(𝒟T,𝒲T)→YT.\displaystyle\qquad\to\dots\to\bigl\{\mathtt{H}\big(p^{\Pi_{k}}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid Y_{T-1})\big)\bigr\}_{k=W_{T-1}+1}^{L}\to(\mathcal{D}_{T},\mathcal{W}_{T})\to Y_{T}. (11)

Theoretical guarantee.

We now present the performance guarantee of the maximum entropy-based inference scheme (Algorithm 2) in Theorem 2 below. The proof can be found in Appendix B.

Theorem 2.

Assume that the mask predictor pθp_{\theta} is optimal, namely, pθ=∏i=1Lpip_{\theta}=\prod_{i=1}^{L}p^{i} is the product of true conditional marginals. For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, set the entropy threshold to η=ε​H​(X0)/L\eta=\sqrt{{\varepsilon H(X_{0})}/{L}} and the maximum unmasking size to Smax=⌊ε​L/H⁡(X0)⌋∨1S_{\max}=\lfloor\sqrt{{\varepsilon L}/{H(X_{0})}}\rfloor\vee 1. Then the maximum entropy-based unmasking strategy in Algorithm 2 achieves ε\varepsilon-accurate sampling in KL divergence, namely, 𝔼Π[𝖪𝖫(pX0∥pYT|Π)]≤ε.\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}\big[\mathsf{KL}(p_{X_{0}}\parallel p_{Y_{T}\mid\Pi})\big]\leq\varepsilon. Moreover, the expected number of iterations satisfies

𝔼⁡[T]≤2​H⁡(X0)​Lε+1.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[T]\leq 2\sqrt{\frac{H(X_{0})L}{\varepsilon}}+1. (12)

In words, the maximum entropy-based decoding strategy attains ε\varepsilon-accuracy in KL divergence with an expected number of iterations scaling as

O⁡(H⁡(X0)​Lε).\displaystyle O\bigg(\sqrt{\frac{H(X_{0})L}{\varepsilon}}\bigg). (13)

As a consequence, when the entropy of the target data distribution satisfies H⁡(X0)≪LH(X_{0})\ll L, it achieves a sublinear iteration complexity in the sequence length LL, thereby implying a provable speedup over fully sequential generation.

Nevertheless, compared with the entropy sum-based strategy, this maximum entropy-based strategy has two important shortcomings:

  • •

    In the parallel sampling regime, where the iteration complexity is smaller than the sequence length LL, the bound in (13) is worse than that in (10) by a factor of ε​L/H⁡(X0)≫1\sqrt{\varepsilon L/H(X_{0})}\gg 1.

  • •

    The parameter choices η\eta and SmaxS_{\max} needed to achieve a sublinear iteration complexity require explicit knowledge of the entropy H⁡(X0)H(X_{0}) of the target data distribution. This stands in stark contrast to the entropy sum-based strategy, which is fully distribution-adaptive.

Since the theoretical guarantees for these two entropy-based decoding strategies are established under the same analysis framework, comparing them suggests that the choice of entropy criterion plays a critical role in efficient entropy-based decoding. An important future direction is thus to develop a deeper understanding of how different entropy criteria affect the sampling performance of DLMs, for example, by deriving algorithm-dependent lower bounds on the iteration complexity of various decoding strategies.

4 Analysis

In this section, we outline the proof strategy for the main theory (Theorem 1) for the entropy sum-based decoding strategy.

4.1 Preliminary facts

Before presenting the proof sketch, we collect several basic facts and notational conventions that will be used throughout the analysis.

Iterate representation.

Starting from the fully masked initialization Y0=(𝖬,…,𝖬)Y_{0}=(\mathsf{M},\dots,\mathsf{M}), the iterate YtY_{t} at step tt is completely characterized by the cumulative unmasking set 𝒲t\mathcal{W}_{t} together with the revealed token values on that set, namely Yt𝒲tY^{\mathcal{W}_{t}}_{t}, since Yti=𝖬Y^{i}_{t}=\mathsf{M} for all i∈𝒲tci\in\mathcal{W}_{t}^{\mathrm{c}}. Thus, the entropy-based sampler can be equivalently viewed as iteratively filling in the coordinates indexed by 𝒲t\mathcal{W}_{t}. To simplify notation, we suppress the time index tt in the iterate YtY_{t} whenever it is clear from context, and we also write X=X0X=X_{0}.

Permutation-induced order.

Given a fixed permutation Π\Pi of [L][L], the sampler scans token indices in the order Π1,Π2,…,ΠL\Pi_{1},\Pi_{2},\ldots,\Pi_{L}, where Πk\Pi_{k} denotes the index of the kk-th token to be unmasked. Let Π−1\Pi^{-1} denote the inverse permutation so that Πi−1=k\Pi^{-1}_{i}=k gives the unmasking order kk of the token with index ii. Moreover, for each token index i∈[L]i\in[L], there exists a unique iteration tit_{i} at which token ii is unmasked, that is, the iteration satisfying i∈𝒟ti=𝒲ti∖𝒲ti−1i\in\mathcal{D}_{t_{i}}=\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}}\setminus\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1}.

Unmasking sets.

The entropy-based sampling procedure produces an increasing sequence of cumulative unmasking sets ∅=𝒲0⊆𝒲1⊆⋯⊆𝒲T=[L]\varnothing=\mathcal{W}_{0}\subseteq\mathcal{W}_{1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathcal{W}_{T}=[L] where TT is the random total number of iterations. For convenience of analysis, we extend this sequence by defining 𝒲t≔[L]\mathcal{W}_{t}\coloneqq[L] for t>Tt>T so that the sequence (𝒲t)t=0L(\mathcal{W}_{t})_{t=0}^{L} is defined for all 0≤t≤L0\leq t\leq L. The incremental unmasking sets (𝒟t)t=1L(\mathcal{D}_{t})_{t=1}^{L} are extended in an analogous manner by setting 𝒟t≔∅\mathcal{D}_{t}\coloneqq\varnothing for t>Tt>T.

In addition, since tokens are revealed according to the permutation order, the cumulative unmasking set at iteration tt can be expressed as

𝒲t={Π1,…,ΠWt},\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{t}=\{\Pi_{1},\ldots,\Pi_{W_{t}}\}, (14)

where we recall the notation Wt≔|𝒲t|W_{t}\coloneqq|\mathcal{W}_{t}|. Equivalently, the unmasking set 𝒲t\mathcal{W}_{t} consists of the first WtW_{t} indices in the permutation Π\Pi. Similarly, the set of newly unmasked tokens at iteration tt can be written as

𝒟t=𝒲t∖𝒲t−1={ΠWt−1+1,…,ΠWt}.\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{t}=\mathcal{W}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{W}_{t-1}=\{\Pi_{W_{t-1}+1},\ldots,\Pi_{W_{t}}\}. (15)

Dependence structure of sampling process.

Finally, we record two critical consequences of the Markovian structure of the entropy sum-based sampling procedure as shown in (8).

  • •

    First, for a fixed permutation Π\Pi, the unmasking set 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} at iteration tt, and hence the cumulative unmasking set 𝒲t\mathcal{W}_{t}, are completely determined by the cumulative set 𝒲t−1\mathcal{W}_{t-1} and sampled token values Y𝒲t−1=(YΠ1,…,YΠ|𝒲t−1|)Y^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}}=(Y^{\Pi_{1}},\dots,Y^{\Pi_{|\mathcal{W}_{t-1}|}}) from the previous iteration.

  • •

    Second, once the permutation Π\Pi and the fully sampled token sequence Y=(Y1,…,YL)∈𝕏LY=(Y^{1},\ldots,Y^{L})\in\mathbb{X}^{L} are given, the entire sampling trajectory is uniquely determined. In particular, one can recover the total number of iterations TT, the cumulative unmasking sets (𝒲t)t=0L(\mathcal{W}_{t})_{t=0}^{L}, and the incremental unmasking sets (𝒟t)t=1L(\mathcal{D}_{t})_{t=1}^{L}. In other words, the total number of iterations TT and sets (𝒲t−1,𝒟t)t=1L(\mathcal{W}_{t-1},\mathcal{D}_{t})_{t=1}^{L} are deterministic functions of the sampled token sequence YY and permutation Π\Pi, i.e.,

    T=T⁡(Y,Π)and𝒲t−1=𝒲t−1​(Y,Π),𝒟t=𝒟t​(Y,Π),t∈[L].\displaystyle T=T(Y,\Pi)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{W}_{t-1}=\mathcal{W}_{t-1}(Y,\Pi),\quad\mathcal{D}_{t}=\mathcal{D}_{t}(Y,\Pi),\quad t\in[L]. (16)

4.2 Proof sketch of Theorem 1

Having introduced the necessary preliminaries, we now outline the proof of Theorem 1 for the entropy sum-based decoding strategy.

Step 1: Express KL error along unmasking trajectory.

We begin by expressing both the sampled distribution and the data distribution along the adaptive unmasking trajectory. The key insight is that, by the characterization in (16), once the permutation π\pi and the sampled sequence xx are given, the realized total iteration count τ\tau and the realized sets (wt−1,dt)t=1L(w_{t-1},d_{t})_{t=1}^{L} are fully determined.

Concretely, when the mask predictor is optimal, conditioned on a fixed permutation Π=π\Pi=\pi, the entropy-based sampler generates the tokens in each unmasking set independently according to the true conditional marginals pθi=pip^{i}_{\theta}=p^{i} defined in (4). Hence the density of the sampled distribution factorizes within each batch as a product of conditional marginals:

log⁡pYT|Π=π​(x)\displaystyle\log p_{Y_{T}\mid\Pi=\pi}(x) =∑t=1τ∑i∈dtlogp(xi∣xwt−1)=∑t=1L𝟙{t≤τ}∑i∈dtlogp(xi∣xwt−1),x∈𝕏L,\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}\sum_{i\in d_{t}}\log p(x^{i}\mid x^{w_{t-1}})=\sum_{t=1}^{L}\mathds{1}\{t\leq\tau\}\sum_{i\in d_{t}}\log p(x^{i}\mid x^{w_{t-1}}),\quad x\in\mathbb{X}^{L}, (17a)
where the total number of iterations τ=τ⁡(x,π)\tau=\tau(x,\pi) and the sets dt=dt​(x,π)d_{t}=d_{t}(x,\pi) and wt−1=wt−1​(x,π)w_{t-1}=w_{t-1}(x,\pi) for 1≤t≤L1\leq t\leq L are uniquely determined by xx and π\pi.

By contrast, under the data distribution, the tokens revealed at each iteration follow their true conditional joint distribution. Grouping the density according to the same unmasking sets (wt−1,dt)t=1L(w_{t-1},d_{t})_{t=1}^{L} gives

logpX0(x)=∑t=1τlogp(xdt∣xwt−1)=∑t=1L𝟙{t≤τ}logp(xdt∣xwt−1).\displaystyle\log p_{X_{0}}(x)=\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}\log p(x^{d_{t}}\mid x^{w_{t-1}})=\sum_{t=1}^{L}\mathds{1}\{t\leq\tau\}\log p(x^{d_{t}}\mid x^{w_{t-1}}). (17b)

Using the two factorizations above, let us calculate the KL divergence between the data and sampled distributions. Fixing a permutation Π=π\Pi=\pi, we can combine (17a) and (17b) to derive

𝖪𝖫(pX0∥pYT|Π=π)\displaystyle\mathsf{KL}\big(p_{X_{0}}\parallel p_{Y_{T}\mid\Pi=\pi}\big)
=𝔼X∼pX0[∑t=1L𝟙{t≤T}logp⁡(X𝒟t∣X𝒲t−1)∏i∈𝒟tp⁡(Xi∣X𝒲t−1)|Π=π]\displaystyle\quad=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim p_{X_{0}}}\Bigg[\sum_{t=1}^{L}\mathds{1}\{t\leq T\}\log\frac{p(X^{\mathcal{D}_{t}}\mid X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}})}{\prod_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{t}}p(X^{i}\mid X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}})}\,\Big|\,\Pi=\pi\Bigg]
=𝔼[∑t=1L𝟙{t≤T}𝔼[logp⁡(X𝒟t∣X𝒲t−1)∏i∈𝒟tp⁡(Xi∣X𝒲t−1)|𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1,Π=π]|Π=π],\displaystyle\quad=\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\sum_{t=1}^{L}\mathds{1}\{t\leq T\}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\log\frac{p(X^{\mathcal{D}_{t}}\mid X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}})}{\prod_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{t}}p(X^{i}\mid X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}})}\,\Big|\,\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}},\Pi=\pi\bigg]\,\big|\,\Pi=\pi\Bigg], (18)

where the last line holds due to the tower property, linearity of expectation, and the fact that {t≤T}={𝒲t−1≠[L]}\{t\leq T\}=\{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}\neq[L]\} can be determined by 𝒲t−1\mathcal{W}_{t-1}. Importantly, the only randomness here (with Π=π\Pi=\pi fixed) comes from X∼pX0X\sim p_{X_{0}}. Once XX is fixed, the iteration count TT, the sets (𝒲t−1,𝒟t)t=1L(\mathcal{W}_{t-1},\mathcal{D}_{t})_{t=1}^{L} and the subsequences (X𝒲t−1,X𝒟t)t=1L(X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}},X^{\mathcal{D}_{t}})_{t=1}^{L} are all determined.

We next study the inner conditional expectation, which corresponds to the contribution of iteration tt to the overall KL sampling error. Fix an iteration t∈[L]t\in[L], and condition on Π=π\Pi=\pi and (𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1)=(wt−1,xwt−1)(\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}})=(w_{t-1},x^{w_{t-1}}). Under this conditioning, the set 𝒟t=dt\mathcal{D}_{t}=d_{t} is deterministic, and we can derive

𝔼[logp⁡(Xdt∣Xwt−1)∏i∈dtp⁡(Xi∣Xwt−1)|(𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1)=(wt−1,xwt−1),Π=π]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigg[\log\frac{p(X^{d_{t}}\mid X^{w_{t-1}})}{\prod_{i\in d_{t}}p(X^{i}\mid X^{w_{t-1}})}\,\Big|\,(\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}})=(w_{t-1},x^{w_{t-1}}),\Pi=\pi\bigg]
=(i)𝔼Xdt[logp⁡(Xdt∣xwt−1)∏i∈dtp⁡(Xi∣xwt−1)|(𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1)=(wt−1,xwt−1),Π=π]\displaystyle\qquad\overset{(\mathrm{i})}{=}\mathbb{E}_{X^{d_{t}}}\bigg[\log\frac{p(X^{d_{t}}\mid x^{w_{t-1}})}{\prod_{i\in d_{t}}p(X^{i}\mid x^{w_{t-1}})}\,\Big|\,(\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}})=(w_{t-1},x^{w_{t-1}}),\Pi=\pi\bigg]
=(ii)𝖪𝖫(pdt(⋅∣xwt−1)∥∏i∈dtpi(⋅∣xwt−1)),\displaystyle\qquad\overset{(\mathrm{ii})}{=}\mathsf{KL}\Big(p^{d_{t}}(\cdot\mid x^{w_{t-1}})\,\big\|\,\prod_{i\in d_{t}}p^{i}(\cdot\mid x^{w_{t-1}})\Big), (19)

where (i) is true because the unmasking set 𝒟t=dt\mathcal{D}_{t}=d_{t} becomes deterministic conditioned on Π=π\Pi=\pi and (𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1)=(wt−1,xwt−1)(\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}})=(w_{t-1},x^{w_{t-1}}); (ii) holds because the expectation is taken with respect to XdtX^{d_{t}} under the true conditional distribution p(⋅∣xwt−1)p(\cdot\mid x^{w_{t-1}}), which is independent of Π\Pi.

Substituting (19) into (18) and then averaging over both X∼pX0X\sim p_{X_{0}} and Π\Pi yields

𝔼Π[𝖪𝖫(pX0∥pYT|Π)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}\big[\mathsf{KL}(p_{X_{0}}\parallel p_{Y_{T}\mid\Pi})\big] =𝔼Π,X∼pX0[∑t=1T𝖪𝖫(p𝒟t(⋅∣X𝒲t−1)∥∏i∈𝒟tpi(⋅∣X𝒲t−1))].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi,X\sim p_{X_{0}}}\Bigg[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathsf{KL}\Big(p^{\mathcal{D}_{t}}(\cdot\mid X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}})\,\big\|\,\prod_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{t}}p^{i}(\cdot\mid X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}})\Big)\Bigg]. (20)

Thus, the expected KL sampling error decomposes as a sum over iterations tt, where each term measures the discrepancy between the true conditional joint distribution of the tokens unmasked at iteration tt and the product of their conditional marginals.

Step 2: Decompose KL error into sum of mutual information.

In light of the expression for the total KL error in (20), it suffices to analyze the contribution from each iteration. This reduces to understanding the KL divergence between a joint distribution and the product of its marginals.

To this end, Lemma 1 below states that this KL divergence can be decomposed into a sum of mutual information terms, each involving one token and the tokens with larger indices. The proof can be found in Appendix A.1.

Lemma 1.

Consider a random sequence (Z1,…,Zd)(Z^{1},\ldots,Z^{d}) with joint distribution pZ1,…,Zdp_{Z^{1},\ldots,Z^{d}} and marginal distributions pZip_{Z^{i}} for i∈[d]i\in[d]. The KL divergence between the joint distribution and the product of marginals is given by

𝖪𝖫(pZ1,…,Zd∥∏i∈[d]pZi)\displaystyle\mathsf{KL}\Big(p_{Z^{1},\ldots,Z^{d}}\,\big\|\,\prod_{i\in[d]}p_{Z^{i}}\Big) =∑i=1d−1I⁡(Zi,Zi+1,Zi+2,…,Zd).\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}I(Z^{i};Z^{i+1},Z^{i+2},\dots,Z^{d}). (21)

Moreover, for any j∈[d]j\in[d], the KL divergence can be upper bounded as

𝖪𝖫(pZ1,…,Zd∥∏i=1dpZi)\displaystyle\mathsf{KL}\Big(p_{Z^{1},\ldots,Z^{d}}\,\big\|\,\prod_{i=1}^{d}p_{Z^{i}}\Big) ≤∑i∈[d]∖{j}I⁡(Zi,Z1,…,Zi−1,Zi+1​…,Zd).\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i\in[d]\setminus\{j\}}I(Z^{i};Z^{1},\dots,Z^{i-1},Z^{i+1}\dots,Z^{d}). (22)
Remark 2.

Both expressions involve a sum of d−1d-1 terms, but they differ in structure. In the identity (21), the last index i=di=d is excluded, and each term measures the mutual information between ZiZ^{i} and the variables with larger indices Zi+1,Zi+2,…,ZdZ^{i+1},Z^{i+2},\dots,Z^{d}. In the upper bound (22), one instead excludes an arbitrary index j∈[d]j\in[d], and each remaining term measures the mutual information between ZiZ^{i} and all other variables ZkZ^{k} with k≠ik\neq i.

We shall apply the upper bound (22) in Lemma 1 to control the per-iteration KL sampling error. The key point is that, by construction, each iteration stops as soon as the running entropy sum of the currently unmasked tokens exceeds the threshold η\eta. Consequently, within each iteration, there can be at most one token whose entropy is larger than η\eta. Motivated by this observation, define

jt\displaystyle j_{t} ≔arg​maxi∈𝒟t⁡𝙷​(Xi∣𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1),\displaystyle\coloneqq\argmax_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{t}}\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}}), (23)

with ties broken arbitrarily. Then every index i∈𝒟t∖{jt}i\in\mathcal{D}_{t}\setminus\{j_{t}\} satisfies

𝙷⁡(Xi∣𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1)≤η.\displaystyle\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}})\leq\eta.

Here, we remind the reader that 𝙷⁡(X∣Z)\mathtt{H}(X\mid Z) denotes the entropy of XX conditioned on a realization of ZZ (without taking the expectation of ZZ), so it is a function of ZZ. Similarly, 𝙸⁡(X;YT∣Z)\mathtt{I}(X;Y_{T}\mid Z) denotes the mutual information between XX and YY given a realization of ZZ.

Now applying (22) in Lemma 1 with pZ1,…,Zd=pDt(⋅∣xwt−1)p_{Z^{1},\ldots,Z^{d}}=p^{D_{t}}(\cdot\mid x^{w_{t-1}}) and j=jtj=j_{t}, we obtain

𝖪𝖫(p𝒟t(⋅∣X𝒲t−1)∥∏i∈𝒟tpi(⋅∣X𝒲t−1))\displaystyle\mathsf{KL}\Big(p^{\mathcal{D}_{t}}(\cdot\mid X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}})\,\big\|\,\prod_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{t}}p^{i}(\cdot\mid X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}})\Big)
≤∑i∈𝒟t𝙸(Xi;X𝒟t∖{i}∣𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1,Π) 1{i≠jt}\displaystyle\quad\leq\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{t}}\mathtt{I}(X^{i};X^{\mathcal{D}_{t}\setminus\{i\}}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}},\Pi)\,\mathds{1}{\{i\neq j_{t}\}}
=∑i∈𝒟t𝙸(Xi;X𝒟t∖{i}∣𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1,Π) 1{𝙷(Xi∣𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1)≤η}.\displaystyle\quad=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{t}}\mathtt{I}(X^{i};X^{\mathcal{D}_{t}\setminus\{i\}}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}},\Pi)\,\mathds{1}{\big\{\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}})\leq\eta\big\}}. (24)
Remark 3.

Conditioned on 𝒲t−1\mathcal{W}_{t-1} and X𝒲t−1X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}}, the conditional entropy 𝙷⁡(Xi∣𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1)\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}}) is independent of the permutation Π\Pi, i.e.,

𝙷⁡(Xi∣𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1)=𝙷⁡(Xi∣𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1,Π).\displaystyle\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}})=\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}},\Pi).

This is in contrast to the mutual information terms, which depend explicitly on the unmasking set 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}, and hence on Π\Pi.

Thus, the KL sampling error contributed by iteration tt is controlled by a sum of mutual information, where each term quantifies the dependence between one unmasked token and the rest of the tokens unmasked in iteration tt, conditioned on the tokens revealed previously. The indicator function in (24) highlights an important feature of the entropy-sum stopping rule: within each iteration, only tokens with conditional entropy at most η\eta contribute to this KL error bound. As will be clear momentarily, this indicator function will be essential in the subsequent analysis.

Substituting the bound (24) into the KL error expression in (20), we find

𝔼Π[𝖪𝖫(pX0∥pYT|Π)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}\Big[\mathsf{KL}\big(p_{X_{0}}\parallel p_{Y_{T}\mid\Pi}\big)\Big] ≤𝔼X,Π[∑t=1T∑i∈𝒟t𝙸(Xi;X𝒟t∖{i}∣𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1,Π) 1{𝙷(Xi∣𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1)≤η}]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{X,\Pi}\Bigg[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{t}}\mathtt{I}(X^{i};X^{\mathcal{D}_{t}\setminus\{i\}}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}},\Pi)\,\mathds{1}{\big\{\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}})\leq\eta\big\}}\Bigg]
=∑i=1L𝔼X,Π[𝙸(Xi;X𝒟ti∖{i}∣𝒲ti−1,X𝒲ti−1,Π) 1{𝙷(Xi∣𝒲ti−1,X𝒲ti−1)≤η}],\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}_{X,\Pi}\Big[\mathtt{I}(X^{i};X^{\mathcal{D}_{t_{i}}\setminus\{i\}}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1}},\Pi)\,\mathds{1}{\big\{\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1}})\leq\eta\big\}}\Big], (25)

where the last step rearranges the summation order from the iteration index tt to the token index ii, where we recall that tit_{i} denotes the index of the iteration at which token ii is unmasked.

In summary, the expected KL sampling error is bounded by a sum of mutual information terms over token index i∈[L]i\in[L]. Each term measures the dependence between token ii and the other unmasked tokens in the same iteration, conditioned on the already unmasked tokens and the permutation.

Step 3: Average over random unmasking order.

Equipped with the KL error bound in (25), it remains to control each token-wise contribution separately.

To this end, fix a token index ii and consider the corresponding summand:

𝔼X,Π∖i,Πi−1[𝙸(Xi;X𝒟ti∖{i}∣𝒲ti−1,X𝒲ti−1,Π)𝟙{𝙷(Xi∣𝒲ti−1,X𝒲ti−1)≤η}].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{X,\Pi_{\smallsetminus i},\Pi^{-1}_{i}}\Big[\mathtt{I}(X^{i};X^{\mathcal{D}_{t_{i}}\setminus\{i\}}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1}},\Pi)\mathds{1}{\big\{\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1}})\leq\eta\big\}}\Big]. (26)

To make the dependence on the permutation explicit, we decompose the randomness of Π\Pi into the position Πi−1\Pi^{-1}_{i} of token ii in the permutation Π\Pi and the relative ordering of all other tokens, denoted by Π∖i\Pi_{\smallsetminus i}. Concretely, we define

Π∖i≔(Π1,…,ΠΠi−1−1,ΠΠi−1+1,…,ΠL).\displaystyle\Pi_{\smallsetminus i}\coloneqq\big(\Pi_{1},\dots,\Pi_{\Pi^{-1}_{i}-1},\Pi_{\Pi^{-1}_{i}+1},\dots,\Pi_{L}\big). (27)

That is, the permutation Π∖i\Pi_{\smallsetminus i} is obtained from Π\Pi by removing the index ii while preserving the relative order of all other tokens.

Our goal is to show, after averaging over the randomness of the position Πi−1\Pi^{-1}_{i}, the contribution of token ii to the KL sampling error admits a clean and tractable upper bound. However, the major technical difficulty arises from the complicated dependence between the set 𝒟ti∖{i}\mathcal{D}_{t_{i}}\setminus\{i\}—the tokens revealed in the same iteration as token ii—and the full permutation Π\Pi. In particular, the iteration index tit_{i} and the set 𝒟ti\mathcal{D}_{t_{i}} both vary with Πi−1\Pi^{-1}_{i}, making it challenging to directly analyze (26).

To address this, recall that Dt≔|𝒟t|D_{t}\coloneqq|\mathcal{D}_{t}| denotes the size of the unmasking set 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} at iteration t∈[L]t\in[L]. We then introduce a sequence of dyadic size envelopes (D¯t)t=1L(\overline{D}_{t})_{t=1}^{L} in ℝ\mathbb{R}, defined recursively by D¯1=0\overline{D}_{1}=0 and, for 2≤t≤L2\leq t\leq L,

D¯t≔{D¯t−1,if​Dt−1<D¯t−1,2​Dt−1,if​Dt−1≥D¯t−1.\displaystyle\overline{D}_{t}\coloneqq\begin{cases}\overline{D}_{t-1},&\text{if}~~D_{t-1}<\overline{D}_{t-1},\\ 2D_{t-1},&\text{if}~~D_{t-1}\geq\overline{D}_{t-1}.\end{cases} (28)

In essence, the envelope remains unchanged as long as the previous set size stays below it; once the previous set size reaches the envelope, the envelope is doubled.

Using the size-envelopes constructed above, the following lemma shows that, after averaging over the random position of token ii, the mutual-information term in (26) can be bounded by a much simpler quantity involving only the conditional entropy of XiX^{i} and the event that the corresponding set size crosses the envelope. The proof is deferred to Appendix A.2.

Lemma 2.

For any token index i∈[L]i\in[L], we have

𝔼X,Π∖i,Πi−1[𝙸(Xi;X𝒟ti∖{i}∣𝒲ti−1,X𝒲ti−1,Π)𝟙{𝙷(Xi∣𝒲ti−1,X𝒲ti−1)≤η}]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{X,\Pi_{\smallsetminus i},\Pi^{-1}_{i}}\Big[\mathtt{I}(X^{i};X^{\mathcal{D}_{t_{i}}\setminus\{i\}}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1}},\Pi)\mathds{1}{\big\{\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1}})\leq\eta\big\}}\Big]
≤2𝔼X,Π∖i[(𝙷(Xi∣𝒲ti−1,X𝒲ti−1)∧η)𝟙{Dti≥D¯ti}].\displaystyle\qquad\leq 2\,\mathbb{E}_{X,\Pi_{\smallsetminus i}}\Big[\big(\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1}})\wedge\eta\big)\mathds{1}\big\{D_{t_{i}}\geq\overline{D}_{t_{i}}\big\}\Big]. (29)

In words, after averaging over the random unmasking order of token ii, its contribution to the KL sampling error is controlled by its truncated conditional entropy, and contributes only on the event that the size of its unmasking set is at least as large as the corresponding envelope. Thus, the intricate dependence structure in (26) is reduced to a much more tractable indicator of whether a size-doubling event occurs.

Step 4: Control KL error by entropy-based stopping rule.

Summing the bound (29) from Lemma 2 over all tokens and combining it with the KL error expression in (25), we obtain

𝔼Π[𝖪𝖫(pX0∥pYT|Π)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}\big[\mathsf{KL}(p_{X_{0}}\parallel p_{Y_{T}\mid\Pi})\big] ≤2𝔼[∑i=1L(𝙷(Xi∣𝒲ti−1,X𝒲ti−1,Π∖i)∧η)𝟙{Dti≥D¯ti}].\displaystyle\leq 2\,\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\sum_{i=1}^{L}\big(\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1}},\Pi_{\smallsetminus i})\wedge\eta\big)\mathds{1}\big\{D_{t_{i}}\geq\overline{D}_{t_{i}}\big\}\Bigg]. (30)

We now reindex the sum by iteration rather than token. Since 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} is exactly the set of tokens revealed at iteration tt, the right-hand side of (30) becomes

𝔼[∑i=1L(𝙷(Xi∣𝒲ti−1,X𝒲ti−1,Π∖i)∧η)𝟙{Dti≥D¯ti}]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\sum_{i=1}^{L}\big(\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1}},\Pi_{\smallsetminus i})\wedge\eta\big)\mathds{1}\big\{D_{t_{i}}\geq\overline{D}_{t_{i}}\big\}\Bigg]
=𝔼[∑t=1L𝟙{Dt≥D¯t}∑i∈𝒟t(𝙷(Xi∣𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1,Π∖i)∧η)]\displaystyle\qquad=\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\sum_{t=1}^{L}\mathds{1}\{D_{t}\geq\overline{D}_{t}\}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{t}}\big(\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}},\Pi_{\smallsetminus i})\wedge\eta\big)\Bigg]

Next, we bound the inner sum using the stopping rule. By construction, within each iteration the cumulative entropy remains below η\eta until the final token is added. Therefore, the total contribution of all but the last token is at most η\eta, while the final token contributes at most η\eta after truncation. Consequently,

∑i∈𝒟t(𝙷⁡(Xi∣𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1,Π∖i)∧η)≤2​η,\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{t}}\big(\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}},\Pi_{\smallsetminus i})\wedge\eta\big)\leq 2\eta,

and hence

𝔼[∑i=1L(𝙷(Xi∣𝒲ti−1,X𝒲ti−1,Π∖i)∧η)𝟙{Dti≥D¯ti}]≤2η⋅𝔼[∑t=1L𝟙{Dt≥D¯t}].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\sum_{i=1}^{L}\big(\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t_{i}-1}},\Pi_{\smallsetminus i})\wedge\eta\big)\mathds{1}\big\{D_{t_{i}}\geq\overline{D}_{t_{i}}\big\}\Bigg]\leq 2\eta\cdot\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\sum_{t=1}^{L}\mathds{1}\{D_{t}\geq\overline{D}_{t}\}\Bigg]. (31)

It remains to bound the number of iterations for which the event Dt≥D¯tD_{t}\geq\overline{D}_{t} occurs. Let s1<s2<…s_{1}<s_{2}<\dots be the iterations at which this event holds. By the definition of the size-envelope sequence in (28), whenever Dsj≥D¯sjD_{s_{j}}\geq\overline{D}_{s_{j}} occurs, the envelope at the next such iteration must have doubled. Thus, we have

Dsj+1≥D¯sj+1=2​Dsj,D_{s_{j+1}}\geq\overline{D}_{s_{j+1}}=2D_{s_{j}},

and by induction,

Dsj≥2j−1​Ds1=2j−1.D_{s_{j}}\geq 2^{j-1}D_{s_{1}}=2^{j-1}.

Since Dsj≤LD_{s_{j}}\leq L for all jj, this implies that the number of such iterations satisfies

∑t=1L𝟙{Dt≥D¯t}≤log2L+1.\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{L}\mathds{1}\{D_{t}\geq\overline{D}_{t}\}\leq\log_{2}L+1. (32)

Finally, combining (30)–(32) gives the final bound on the expected KL sampling error:

𝔼Π[𝖪𝖫(pX0∥pYT|Π)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}\big[\mathsf{KL}(p_{X_{0}}\parallel p_{Y_{T}\mid\Pi})\big] ≤4​η​(log2⁡L+1).\displaystyle\leq 4\eta(\log_{2}L+1). (33)

Setting η=ε/(4​(log2⁡L+1))\eta=\varepsilon/(4(\log_{2}L+1)) immediately yields the desired result 𝔼Π[𝖪𝖫(pX0∥pYT|Π)]≤ε\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}\big[\mathsf{KL}(p_{X_{0}}\parallel p_{Y_{T}\mid\Pi})\big]\leq\varepsilon.

Step 5: Bound expected number of iterations.

Finally, let us study the expected number of iterations 𝔼⁡[T]\mathbb{E}[T]. To this end, we use the following entropy identity, whose proof is deferred to Appendix A.3.

Lemma 3.

For any fixed permutation Π\Pi, the entropy of the data distribution admits the following decomposition:

H⁡(X0)\displaystyle H(X_{0}) =𝔼X∼pX0​[∑t=1T𝙷⁡(X𝒟t∣𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1,Π)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim p_{X_{0}}}\Bigg[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathtt{H}(X^{\mathcal{D}_{t}}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}},\Pi)\Bigg] (34)
=𝔼X∼pX0[∑t=1T∑i∈𝒟t𝙷(Xi∣𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1,Π)]−𝖪𝖫(pX0∥pYT|Π).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim p_{X_{0}}}\Bigg[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{t}}\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}},\Pi)\Bigg]-\mathsf{KL}(p_{X_{0}}\parallel p_{Y_{T}\mid\Pi}). (35)

We now combine this identity with the stopping rule. By construction, every iteration except the last one accumulates conditional entropy at least η\eta, that is,

∑i∈𝒟t𝙷⁡(Xi∣𝒲t−1,X𝒲t−1,Π)≥η,\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{t}}\mathtt{H}(X^{i}\mid\mathcal{W}_{t-1},X^{\mathcal{W}_{t-1}},\Pi)\geq\eta,

for all t<Tt<T. Therefore, substituting this into the entropy identity (35) yields

H(X0)≥𝔼[T−1]η−𝔼Π[𝖪𝖫(pX0∥pYT|Π)].\displaystyle H(X_{0})\geq\mathbb{E}[T-1]\eta-\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}\big[\mathsf{KL}(p_{X_{0}}\parallel p_{Y_{T}\mid\Pi})\big].

Using the KL bound from (33), we further obtain

H⁡(X0)≥(𝔼⁡[T]−1−4​(log2⁡L+1))​η.\displaystyle H(X_{0})\geq\big(\mathbb{E}[T]-1-4(\log_{2}L+1)\big)\eta.

Therefore, rearranging the above inequality and substituting η=ε/(4​(log2⁡L+1))\eta=\varepsilon/(4(\log_{2}L+1)) into it yields

𝔼⁡[T]≤H⁡(X0)η+4​(log2⁡L+1)+1=4​(H⁡(X0)ε+1)​(log2⁡L+1)+1.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[T]\leq\frac{H(X_{0})}{\eta}+4(\log_{2}L+1)+1=4\bigg(\frac{H(X_{0})}{\varepsilon}+1\bigg)(\log_{2}L+1)+1.

This completes the proof of Theorem 1.

5 Discussion

In this work, we have made progress toward understanding the sampling efficiency of confidence-based decoding strategies in DLMs. Our results show that entropy-based unmasking strategies can provably accelerate sampling, achieving an iteration complexity that is sublinear in the sequence length when the data distribution has low entropy. Notably, they reveal that entropy-based strategies can adapt to the unknown intrinsic complexity of the data distribution without requiring any prior knowledge or hyperparameter tuning.

Moving forward, it would be of interest to understand the performance of the entropy-based decoding schemes based on a deterministic order (e.g., a sorted order) instead of the random order considered in this work. Also, it would be valuable to extend our analysis to more general confidence measures beyond entropy, such as the mass of the most likely token and the mass gap between the two most likely tokens. Second, our current analysis focuses on the scenario where the optimal mask predictor is used. It would be important to understand the impact of training error in the mask predictor on the sampling performance under confidence-based decoding, which may yield insights into the design of more effective training objectives for DLMs. Third, another important direction is to establish lower bounds on the iteration complexity of confidence-based decoding schemes, which would shed light on the fundamental limits of sampling acceleration when using this class of strategies.
